content_list.content_text: The origins of the epic film lie in Europe, and more precisely in Italy, where filmmakers drew inspiration from their country's classical past to make visually extravagant films of operatic proportions. Enrico Guazzoni (1876-1949) used 5,000 extras in his nine-reel drama Quo Vadis? (1912), set in Ancient Rome. Giovanni Pastrone (1883-1959) shot Cabiria (1914) in multiple locations.

The film runs three hours, with a cast of hundreds and spectacular sets. Pastrone and his Spanish cinematographer Segundo de Chomón were the first to use a dolly-on-tracks system so the camera could move, which allowed them to create uninterrupted tracking shots (shots in which the camera moves closer to the subject). De Chomón was a master of special effects, collaborating on Napoléon (Napoleon, 1927), directed by Abel Gance (1889-1981), an epic that explored a variety of filming techniques.

information.contentText: Since the camera can move in the three dimensions of space, one can say there are three types of tracking shot, depending on the axis along which the movement takes place. A lateral tracking shot (to the left or right) is one in which the camera moves parallel to the main subject of the shot. In a forward or backward tracking shot (moving in or pulling out), the camera's movement is perpendicular to the subject. Vertical tracking shots (or crane shots) are those in which the camera moves up or down, usually with the help of a specific piece of equipment called a crane.

content_list.content_text: Italian sword-and-sandal epics were a major influence on Hollywood production and inspired Cecil B. DeMille (1881-1959) to make his first version of The Ten Commandments (1923), a 136-minute spectacle dramatizing the biblical story of Moses. DeMille put his flair to work again in 1927, when he directed the spectacular biblical epic The King of Kings (1927).

When World War I broke out in 1914, the development of the European film industry was interrupted, but American filmmakers kept breaking down the barriers of the seventh art. D. W. Griffith (1875-1948) directed a saga about the American Civil War, The Birth of a Nation (1915), a groundbreaking work in both its technical and narrative style.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Carol King, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

content_list.content_text: At once one of the most revered and most reviled films ever made, D. W. Griffith's The Birth of a Nation matters for the very same reasons that inspire these two opposing reactions. Rarely has a film earned such praise and such contempt, which in many ways increases its value not only in the annals of cinema, but also as a fundamental historical artifact (some would call it a relic).

information.contentTitle: Scene from The Birth of a Nation
information.contentText: On March 21, 1915, Democratic President Woodrow Wilson attended a special screening of The Birth of a Nation. It was the first time a film had been shown at the White House. The president was enchanted after the screening: it was a lavish American production in which heroes, members of the Ku Klux Klan, rescue the damsel from the villains' clutches.

content_list.content_text: Although the film is based on Thomas Dixon's explicitly racist play The Clansman: An Historical Romance of the Ku Klux Klan, accounts claim that Griffith was indifferent to the racist content of its central theme. The degree of the director's complicity in conveying its infamous message has been debated for nearly a century. There is no controversy, however, about the film's technical and artistic merits: Griffith was, as usual, more interested in the possibilities of the medium than in the message, and in that realm he set the standards of modern Hollywood.

The Birth of a Nation was, quite clearly, the first historical epic ever made, proving that, even in the silent film era, audiences were willing to sit through a story more than three hours long. With its countless artistic innovations, Griffith essentially created contemporary film language, and although some elements of The Birth of a Nation may seem dated, virtually every film owes it a debt in some way. Griffith introduced the use of dramatic close-ups, tracking shots and other significant camera movements; parallel action, alternating sequences and other editing techniques; and even the first orchestrated score. It is a pity that all these innovative elements were tied to a story of such dubious merit.

quote.quote: It is the greatest thing I have accomplished, but I will not be satisfied until I do something more... I am, like all human beings, driven by perfection.
quote.author: D. W. Griffith

content_list.content_text: The first half of the film begins before the Civil War, explaining the introduction of slavery in the United States before the action gets underway. Two families are introduced: the Stonemans from the North and the Camerons from the South. The story is told through these families and, often, through their servants, embodying the worst racial stereotypes. As the nation is torn apart by war, the slaves and abolitionist sympathizers are portrayed as the destructive force behind it all.

The film's racism worsens in the second half, which takes place during Reconstruction and depicts the rise of the Ku Klux Klan, whose members are presented as the film's supposed heroes. That Griffith introduced a love story in the middle of this re-creation of a race war is extremely audacious: a choice that is at once thrilling and disturbing.

information.contentText: Members of the N.A.A.C.P. protesting under the marquee of the Republic Movie Theatre in Flushing, New York, against the racial discrimination depicted in the film "The Birth of a Nation," screened at the theater in 1947.

content_list.content_text: The Birth of a Nation is undoubtedly powerful propaganda, even though its political message is stomach-turning. The film seems to say that only the puritanical Ku Klux Klan can preserve the unity of the nation. Not surprisingly, even in its own time the film was met with outrage. It drew protests from the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), sparked demonstrations and later forced Griffith himself to respond to the criticism with his even more ambitious Intolerance: Love's Struggle Throughout the Ages (1916). Still, the fact that The Birth of a Nation is respected and studied to this day — despite its subject matter — reveals its enduring importance.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Joshua Klein, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

movies.title: The Birth of a Nation
movies.overview: Two families, abolitionist Northerners the Stonemans and Southern landowners the Camerons, intertwine. When Confederate colonel Ben Cameron is captured in battle, nurse Elsie Stoneman petitions for his pardon. In Reconstruction-era South Carolina, Cameron founds the Ku Klux Klan, battling Elsie's congressman father and his African-American protégé, Silas Lynch.

movies.title: Quo Vadis?
movies.overview: "Quo Vadis?" was a landmark in early Italian historical epic films, and certainly Enrico Guazzoni’s grand scale masterpiece laid the foundations for what genuine colossal Italian spectacles should be. It had a great deal of influence on Giovanni Pastrone’s "Cabiria" (1914) and D.W. Griffith’s "Intolerance" (1916).

movies.title: Cabiria
movies.overview: Young Cabiria is kidnapped by pirates and sold as a slave in Carthage. Just as she's to be sacrificed to Moloch, Cabiria is rescued by Fulvius Axilla, a good-hearted Roman spy, and his powerful slave, Maciste. The trio are broken up as Cabiria is entrusted to a woman of noble birth. With Cabiria's fate unknown, Maciste punished for his heroism, and Fulvius sent away to fight for Rome, is there any hope of our heroes reuniting?

movies.title: Napoleon
movies.overview: A massive 5 1/2 hour biopic of Napoleon, tracing his career from his schooldays (where a snowball fight is staged like a military campaign), his flight from Corsica, through the French Revolution (where a real storm is intercut with a political storm) and the Terror, culminating in his triumphant invasion of Italy in 1797 (the film stops there because it was intended to be part one of six, but director Abel Gance never raised the money to make the other five). The film's legendary reputation is due to the astonishing range of techniques that Gance uses to tell his story, culminating in the final twenty-minute triptych sequence, which alternates widescreen panoramas with complex multiple- image montages projected simultaneously on three screens.

movies.title: The Last Days of Pompeii
movies.overview: Well respected Pompeiian Glaucus performs an act of kindness by buying Nidia, a blind slave being mistreated by her owner. Nidia falls in love with her new master, but he only has eyes for Jone. Jone in turn is lusted after by Arbace, an Egyptian high priest of Isis. When Nidia beseeches Isis for help in capturing Glaucus' heart, Arbace gives her a "love" potion, which really will affect his mind and not his heart, thus opening the way to Jone for himself. When Arbace's disciple is murdered Glaucus finds himself in hot water, shortly after which Mt. Vesuvius erupts.

movies.title: The Ten Commandments
movies.overview: The first part tells the story of Moses leading the Jews from Egypt to the Promised Land, his receipt of the tablets and the worship of the golden calf. The second part shows the efficacy of the commandments in modern life through a story set in San Francisco. Two brothers, rivals for the love of Mary, also come into conflict when John discovers Dan used shoddy materials to construct a cathedral.

movies.title: The King of Kings
movies.overview: The King of Kings is the Greatest Story Ever Told as only Cecil B. DeMille could tell it. In 1927, working with one of the biggest budgets in Hollywood history, DeMille spun the life and Passion of Christ into a silent-era blockbuster. Featuring text drawn directly from the Bible, a cast of thousands, and the great showman’s singular cinematic bag of tricks, The King of Kings is at once spectacular and deeply reverent—part Gospel, part Technicolor epic.

movies.original_title: Intolerance: Love's Struggle Throughout the Ages
movies.title: Intolerance: Love's Struggle Throughout the Ages
movies.overview: The story of a poor young woman, separated by prejudice from her husband and baby, is interwoven with tales of intolerance from throughout history.

movies.title: Greed
movies.overview: A lottery win of $5,000 forever changes the lives of a miner turned dentist and his wife.

movies.title: Die Nibelungen: Siegfried
movies.overview: Siegfried, son of King Siegmund of Xanten, travels to Worms, capital of the Burgundian kingdom, to ask King Gunther for the hand of his sister, the beautiful Kriemhild.

movies.title: Die Nibelungen: Kriemhilds Rache
movies.overview: When Kriemhild, thirsty for revenge, marries to Etzel, king of the Huns, she invites King Gunther and his court to visit them, intending to finally take the life of the man responsible of her disgrace.
